line: Is the world really going to end tomorrow,
on November {13th|thirteenth}?
Why is everyone saying this?
Because this date wasn't predicted by a mystic,
but was calculated {66|sixty six} years ago
by three scientists
and published in one of the world's
top science magazines.
They wrote that future generations would not die of hunger,
but would be squeezed to death by overcrowding.
The alarming part is
that their formula remained roughly accurate
for the next {30|thirty} years.
But how did a formula predict
the exact end of the world?
Consider this:
it took humanity hundreds of thousands of years
to reach the first {1 billion|one billion} people.
The next {1 billion|one billion}
took just {123|one hundred twenty three} years,
and the one after that
took only {33|thirty three} years.
As the population grew,
so did new ideas—
leading to better medicine,
more food,
lower death rates,
and consequently, even more people.
When the scientists projected this accelerating pace forward,
the interval between population leaps shrank
until it would eventually hit zero.
In other words,
the population would become so immense
that there wouldn't even be room left to stand on Earth.
That calculated date turned out to be
Friday, November
{13, 2026|thirteenth twenty twenty six}.
So, how did we survive?
Those same scientists had also proposed the solution:
the world needed to cut its birth rates in half.
And that is precisely what happened.
Today, the average number of children per woman globally
is about half of what it was in {1960|nineteen sixty},
and in India,
it has dropped from around six to two.
This means their formula wasn't wrong;
humanity simply changed course.
Therefore, the world will not end tomorrow—
it will just be another ordinary Friday.
But suppose tomorrow truly were
the last day on Earth:
what would be the very first thing you would do?
Let us know in the comments.
